Writing a dimension package

Source: vignettes/dimension-package.Rmd
dimension-package.Rmd

What nestedscales is for

Models rarely use data at the resolution it arrives in. Demand comes by hour and the model runs on twelve representative days; statistics come by district and the model has five regions; accounts come by detailed industry and the model has six sectors. Each of these is a scale: a set of fine units, the atoms, grouped into coarser levels, the frames. Hours sit inside days inside months; districts inside provinces inside countries.

nestedscales stores such a hierarchy as a NestedScale and converts data along it: summing extensive quantities, averaging intensive ones with the right weights, splitting coarse values down to fine units, and attaching group labels to a dataset. The same functions work whatever the dimension is, because a scale is just a table of atoms with one column per frame.

library(nestedscales)

Dimension packages

Some dimensions need more than a table. Time has calendars, leap years, fiscal years, and a mapping from clock time to the model’s time slices. Space has maps, geometry and coordinate systems. These live in dimension packages built on nestedscales:

  • timescales provides Calendar, a scale of time: a catalog of standard calendars, conversion from datetimes, calendar plots.
  • geoscales provides Geoscale, a scale of space: region hierarchies from data providers, geometry, maps.

Both classes are subclasses of NestedScale, so each package adds what is special about its dimension and gets the conversion machinery from nestedscales. A Calendar is a NestedScale:

cal <- timescales::calendar("m12_h24") # 12 months x 24 hours
scale_is(cal)
#> [1] TRUE
scale_frames(cal)
#> [1] "MONTH" "HOUR"
head(scale_leaftable(cal), 3)
#>   MONTH HOUR       share weight timeslice
#> 1   m01  h00 0.003538813     31   m01_h00
#> 2   m02  h00 0.003196347     28   m02_h00
#> 3   m03  h00 0.003538813     31   m03_h00

and so is a Geoscale:

gs <- geoscales::geoscale_example()
scale_is(gs)
#> [1] TRUE
scale_frames(gs)
#> [1] "country" "state"   "zone"    "atom"
head(scale_leaftable(gs), 3)
#>   country state zone atom km2 pop region
#> 1       N    N1   N1   A1 100  10     A1
#> 2       N    N1   N1   A2 200  90     A2
#> 3       N    N2   ZB   A3 300  30     A3

so the functions of this package work on either. Hourly load summed to months uses the same recast_scale() as any other scale:

load <- data.frame(timeslice = scale_units(cal), mw = 1)
head(recast_scale(load, cal, from = "timeslice", to = "MONTH", rule = "sum"), 3)
#>   MONTH mw
#> 1   m01 24
#> 2   m02 24
#> 3   m03 24

and the regions of country N come from the same navigation function as anything else:

scale_children(gs, "country", "N")
#> [1] "N1" "N2"

The dimension packages wrap these in their own vocabulary – timescales::recast_calendar(), geoscales::geoscale_children() – but the work underneath is shared.

Do you need a package?

Often not. Any hierarchy that fits in a table can be used directly:

sectors <- data.frame(
  section  = c("C", "C", "C", "D", "D"),
  division = c("C10", "C10", "C24", "D35", "D35"),
  activity = c("C10.1", "C10.5", "C24.1", "D35.1", "D35.2"),
  gva      = c(30, 20, 50, 80, 20)
)
nace <- scale_from_leaftable(sectors,
  frames = c("section", "division", "activity"),
  key = "activity", name = "nace"
)
nace
#> NestedScale: nace
#> Frames (3, coarsest first):
#>   - section (2)
#>     - division (3)
#>       - activity (5)
#> Atoms: 5
#> Weights: gva (default: gva)

Write a dimension package when the dimension has something of its own to offer: standard classifications to ship, its own way of building scales, extra data per atom, plots, or simply a vocabulary its users expect. The rest of this article builds a small one for industry classifications, and shows at each step how timescales and geoscales do the same thing.

Step 1: a subclass

A dimension class is an S7 class whose parent is scale_class(). (The NestedScale class itself is reached this way rather than exported; the package exports functions only.)

Two parts are typical. A constructor fixes what is fixed for the dimension, such as the name of the key column and the weights, and passes the rest to scale_from_leaftable(). An alias property lets users call the frames by the dimension’s own word; scale_alias_property() builds it.

The industry class calls its frames levels, and also keeps a title for each activity:

titles <- data.frame(
  activity = sectors$activity,
  title = c(
    "Meat processing", "Dairy products", "Basic iron and steel",
    "Electric power generation", "Gas distribution"
  )
)

Industry <- S7::new_class(
  "Industry",
  parent = scale_class(),
  properties = list(
    levels = scale_alias_property("frames"),
    titles = S7::class_data.frame
  ),
  constructor = function(leaftable, levels, titles) {
    s <- scale_from_leaftable(leaftable,
      frames = levels, key = "activity",
      weights = "gva", name = "nace"
    )
    S7::new_object(s, titles = titles)
  },
  validator = function(self) {
    if (!all(self@leaftable$activity %in% self@titles$activity)) {
      "every activity needs a title"
    }
  }
)

ind <- Industry(sectors,
  levels = c("section", "division", "activity"),
  titles = titles
)
ind@levels
#> [1] "section"  "division" "activity"

The two dimension packages follow the same pattern. A Calendar calls its frames timeframes and always keys its atoms by timeslice; a Geoscale calls them geoframes, keys them by region, and carries geometry:

# timescales
Calendar <- S7::new_class(
  "Calendar",
  parent = nestedscales::scale_class(),
  properties = list(timeframes = nestedscales::scale_alias_property("frames")),
  ...
)

# geoscales
Geoscale <- S7::new_class(
  "Geoscale",
  parent = nestedscales::scale_class(),
  properties = list(
    geoframes = nestedscales::scale_alias_property("frames"),
    geometry  = S7::new_property(S7::class_any, default = NULL)
  ),
  ...
)

Step 2: the shared functions already work

Nothing more is needed for the industry scale to convert data:

jobs <- data.frame(activity = sectors$activity, jobs = c(5, 3, 8, 2, 1))
recast_scale(jobs, ind,
  from = "activity", to = "section",
  values = "jobs", rule = "sum"
)
#>   section jobs
#> 1       C   16
#> 2       D    3

The same holds for join_scale(), filter_scale(), the navigation functions, scale_product(), clustering and the Arrow store. The generic recast() dispatches on the new class too:

recast(jobs, ind, to = "division", values = "jobs", rule = "sum")
#>   division jobs
#> 1      C10    8
#> 2      C24    8
#> 3      D35    3

Step 3: the dimension’s vocabulary

Error messages from the shared functions are written once and filled in with words from scale_vocab(). Without a method, an industry scale is described in neutral words:

recast_scale(jobs, ind,
  from = "activity", to = "group",
  values = "jobs", rule = "sum"
)
#> Error:
#> ! `to` = "group" is not a frame of this NestedScale; one of: section, division, activity

A method supplies the dimension’s own:

S7::method(scale_vocab, Industry) <- function(x, ...) {
  list(
    object = "Industry", frame = "level", frames = "levels",
    unit = "industry", units = "industries", atoms = "activities"
  )
}

recast_scale(jobs, ind,
  from = "activity", to = "group",
  values = "jobs", rule = "sum"
)
#> Error:
#> ! `to` = "group" is not a level of this Industry; one of: section, division, activity

This is why a calendar’s errors talk about timeframes and a region hierarchy’s about geoframes:

scale_vocab(cal)$frame
#> [1] "timeframe"
recast_scale(load, cal, from = "timeslice", to = "WEEK", rule = "sum")
#> Error:
#> ! `to` = "WEEK" is not a timeframe of this Calendar; one of: MONTH, HOUR, timeslice

The vocabulary may also name the dimension package’s own registration functions (register_rule, register_map), so that a message suggesting one points to, say, register_geoscale_rule() rather than the generic register_scale_rule().

Step 4: data kept per atom

When a function keeps only some atoms – filter_scale(), prune_scale(), x[frame, unit] – the result keeps its class and any extra properties. If those properties hold one entry per atom, a scale_payload_slice() method cuts them down to match:

S7::method(scale_payload_slice, Industry) <- function(x, i, ...) {
  x@titles <- x@titles[x@titles$activity %in% x@leaftable$activity, ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  x
}

manufacturing <- filter_scale(ind, "section", "C")
class(manufacturing)
#> [1] "Industry"                  "nestedscales::NestedScale"
#> [3] "S7_object"
manufacturing@titles
#>   activity                title
#> 1    C10.1      Meat processing
#> 2    C10.5       Dairy products
#> 3    C24.1 Basic iron and steel
scale_coverage(manufacturing)
#> gva 
#> 0.5

geoscales uses the same hook for its geometry, which has one shape per atom in leaftable order, so a filtered Geoscale keeps exactly the shapes of the regions it kept. The object is validated once the hook has run, so the data may be positional, like geometry, or keyed by atom code, like the titles here.

Atoms that are combinations of frames

In the industry scale every activity belongs to one division and every division to one section: the frames nest, and the finest frame lists the atoms. Time does not work that way. In m12_h24 the frames are months and hours of the day; an hour of the day is not inside a month, and the atoms – 288 time slices – are combinations of the two. nestedscales handles this by taking the atoms from the key column when no frame lists them. scale_atom_level() reports which case applies:

scale_atom_level(ind)
#> [1] "activity"
scale_atom_level(cal)
#> [1] "timeslice"
length(scale_units(cal))
#> [1] 288

A dimension whose atoms are combinations of other categories works the same way, with no extra code.

Trees and overlays

Frames do not have to nest. In the industry scale every activity belongs to exactly one division: the frames form a tree. In m12_h24 an hour of the day belongs to every month: the two frames overlay, and the atoms are their combinations. Both are ordinary scales, because every conversion routes through the atoms and a crosswalk carries the overlap of each pair of units; nothing is stored about the relationship between frames. Three queries report the structure a scale actually has:

scale_nests(ind, "division", "activity")   # one parent per activity
#> [1] TRUE
scale_crosses(ind, "division", "activity") # not a product
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"offenders")
#> [1] "C24" "D35"
scale_is_uniform(ind, "division")          # divisions differ in size
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"sizes")
#> C10 C24 D35 
#>   2   1   2
scale_nests(cal, "MONTH", "HOUR")          # an hour belongs to every month
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"offenders")
#>  [1] "h00" "h01" "h02" "h03" "h04" "h05" "h06" "h07" "h08" "h09" "h10" "h11"
#> [13] "h12" "h13" "h14" "h15" "h16" "h17" "h18" "h19" "h20" "h21" "h22" "h23"
scale_crosses(cal, "MONTH", "HOUR")        # the frames form a product
#> [1] TRUE
scale_is_uniform(cal, "MONTH")             # 24 atoms in every month
#> [1] TRUE

What the order of frames does decide is direction. scale_rank() is the position in that vector, and the rules that need a notion of “coarser” use it: "share" needs a parent frame that nests, residuals aggregate upward only, and reconcile_scale() compares against the coarser frame. For a tree the order is forced; for an overlay it is a convention the author sets, and it should list first the frame they think of as the coarser one.

Turning it into a package

Inside a script, methods can be registered directly, as above. A package registers them on the nestedscales generics with S7’s external generics, so that nestedscales finds them without depending on the package:

# R/industry-class.R
.scale_vocab_generic <- S7::new_external_generic(
  "nestedscales",
  "scale_vocab", "x"
)
S7::method(.scale_vocab_generic, Industry) <- function(x, ...) {
  list(
    object = "Industry", frame = "level", frames = "levels",
    unit = "industry", units = "industries", atoms = "activities"
  )
}

# R/zzz.R
.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  S7::methods_register()
}

The DESCRIPTION names nestedscales and S7:

Imports:
    nestedscales,
    S7

Both dimension packages also give recast() a method of their own, because their conversions take extra arguments – timescales needs a year to place a calendar on real dates – and re-export the generic so that library(timescales) or library(geoscales) alone provides it:

.recast_generic <- S7::new_external_generic(
  "nestedscales", "recast",
  c("x", "from")
)
S7::method(.recast_generic, list(S7::class_any, Industry)) <-
  function(x, from, to, ...) {
    recast_scale(x, from, to = to, ...)
  }

#' @importFrom nestedscales recast
#' @export
nestedscales::recast

When a dimension’s conversions cannot be read off one scale’s table – timescales maps one calendar onto another through a grid of real dates – the package builds the correspondence itself and hands it to recast_crosswalk(), which applies the same rules as recast_scale().

Things to keep in mind

  • Test class membership with scale_is(), not by name. Inside an installed package an S7 class is called "yourpackage::Industry", but under pkgload::load_all() it is plain "Industry".
  • Saved objects carry their class. An object saved to data/ or an .rds file records its class and parent. If either changes, the saved object stops being a NestedScale and the shared functions reject it with “x must be a NestedScale object”. Rebuild saved objects after changing a class.
  • Keep dimension-specific code in the dimension package. nestedscales depends on no dimension package, and nothing in it needs to know that calendars or regions exist.
